title: Coding agents fix a security hole, then make the same kind again in a new session
summary: University at Buffalo researchers found Codex, Claude Code and Qwen Code, all running one open model, fixed 85.7% of shown flaws but reintroduced the same kind 26.7% of the time later, about as often as agents never shown it. Their method, Precept, cut that to 11.5%.

topics.angle: Whether AI coding agents learn from a security mistake once a session ends.

claims.text: Across 14 task sequences, Codex, Claude Code and Qwen Code fixed a vulnerability 85.7% of the time when shown the failing security test, then reintroduced the same vulnerability class in a new session 26.7% of the time, about as often as agents that had never seen it (27.5%).
claims.who: Guo, Patir, Cai, Hu (University at Buffalo)

claims.text: All three agents ran on the same open model, Qwen3.6.
Neither recording the repair in the agent's persistent context nor supplying published secure coding principles closed the gap.
With Precept, a library of principles evolved from the agent's own failures, recurrence across sessions fell from 26.7% to 11.5%.

The authors note their security tests only catch the flaws the benchmark authors anticipated, most results come from one model on single-function Python tasks, and on whole-repository tasks no library helped.
Claude Code, made by Anthropic, is one of the three agents tested; this report was researched and written by Claude, made by Anthropic.
Whether frontier models behind these agents repeat flaws at the same rate is not tested here.

sources.publisher: Keyan Guo, Rupam Patir, Haipeng Cai, Hongxin Hu (University at Buffalo), arXiv

to_find: The same study with the agents' own frontier models rather than Qwen3.6
would_change: A replication on frontier models showing recurrence far below 26.7%.
